title: SPF 30, 50, or 100? What Those Sunscreen Numbers Really Mean
summary: Summer is here, and that means sunscreen! But what do those SPF numbers on the bottle actually mean? SPF stands for sun protection factor. It tells you how well a sunscreen protects your skin from UVB rays — the kind that cause sunburns. Dr. Adewole Adamson, a skin doctor, says SPF 30 filters out about 97% of UVB rays. SPF 50 filters about 98%. So doubling the number doesn't double the protection. Even SPF 100 doesn't block everything. In fact, the government banned the word 'sunblock' because no sunscreen can block all rays. Doctors say to use at least SPF 30, but higher is better because most people don't put on enough. If you use too little, you get less protection than the label says. Also, look for 'broad spectrum' on the bottle — that means it guards against UVA rays too, which can also hurt your skin. And if you'll be swimming or sweating, pick a 'water resistant' one. The best sunscreen? The one you'll actually use! 'Find a sunscreen that feels good on your skin,' says Dr. Adamson. So grab your hat, your shades, and your SPF — and have a safe, sunny summer!
why_it_matters: Knowing how to protect your skin from the sun with the right sunscreen helps you enjoy outdoor play and sports safely all summer long.

keywords.explanation: Sun Protection Factor — a number that tells you how well a sunscreen protects your skin from sunburn-causing rays.
A type of sunlight that can burn the top layer of your skin and cause redness or pain.
A label meaning the sunscreen protects against both UVB and UVA rays, not just one kind.
Another type of sunlight that goes deeper into skin and can cause wrinkles and damage over time.
A product that stays on your skin and protects you even if you swim or sweat, for a certain amount of time.
An old word for sunscreen that was banned by the government because no product can block all sunlight completely.

background_read: Dr. Adewole Adamson (a skin doctor who studies how sunlight affects our skin) helps people understand sun safety.
Sunlight contains invisible UV (ultraviolet) rays — UVA and UVB — that can hurt skin even on cloudy days.
The first sunscreen was invented in the 1930s, and since then scientists have been improving how we protect ourselves while enjoying the outdoors.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dr. Adewole Adamson and anyone who uses sunscreen
WHAT: Explaining what SPF numbers really mean and how to pick the right sunscreen
WHERE: Anywhere sunny, like a beach, pool, or park
WHY: So people can avoid sunburns and skin damage while still having fun outside

perspectives.description: Wants a sunscreen that doesn't feel sticky or greasy so they can run and swim without complaining, and might not reapply it often enough.
Recommends at least SPF 30, reminds everyone to use enough lotion, and says the best sunscreen is the one a person will actually use, even if the number is lower.
Sees many sunburns and would advise water-resistant, broad-spectrum sunscreen reapplied every two hours, because water and sweat wash protection away.
